Measure Words.notes: the all-purpose, no-frills measure word
Measure Words.examples: 一个人 | yí ge rén | a person ; 三个苹果 | sān ge píngguǒ | three apples

Measure Words.notes: a more polite/respectful measure word, used for people you're addressing formally or showing respect to. Typical nouns: customers, guests, teachers, doctors, elders
Measure Words.examples: 一位老师 | yí wèi lǎoshī | a teacher ; 两位客人 | liǎng wèi kèrén | two guests

Measure Words.notes: specifically for counting family/household members. an idiom for "mouths to feed"
Measure Words.examples: 我家有五口人 | wǒ jiā yǒu wǔ kǒu rén | there are five people in my family

Measure Words.notes: a more formal/official register, common in news reports, documents, or rosters rather than casual speech
Measure Words.examples: 一名学生 | yì míng xuésheng | a student

Measure Words.notes: for businesses/shops as commercial establishments
Measure Words.examples: 一家餐厅 | yì jiā cāntīng | a restaurant ; 一家公司 | yì jiā gōngsī | a company

Measure Words.notes: used for shops, especially in Taiwan Mandarin, and for rooms in general
Measure Words.examples: 一间卧室 | yì jiān wòshì | a bedroom ; 一间办公室 | yì jiān bàngōngshì | an office

Measure Words.notes: for buildings as physical structures. This is the one for "building" specifically
Measure Words.examples: 一栋公寓楼 | yí dòng gōngyù lóu | an apartment building

Measure Words.notes: for large, substantial structures/facilities. Reach for this with anything big and solid.
Measure Words.examples: 一座动物园 | yí zuò dòngwùyuán | a zoo

Measure Words.notes: specifically for an apartment as a self-contained unit
Measure Words.examples: 一套公寓 | yí tào gōngyù | an apartment/unit

Measure Words.notes: for bound/printed volumes
Measure Words.examples: 一本书 | yì běn shū | a book ; 一本杂志 | yì běn zázhì | a magazine

Measure Words.notes: for flat things with a surface
Measure Words.examples: 一张纸 | yì zhāng zhǐ | a sheet of paper ; 一张桌子 | yì zhāng zhuōzi | a table ; 一张票 | yì zhāng piào | a ticket ; 一张照片 | yì zhāng zhàopiàn | a photo

Measure Words.notes: for long, thin, flexible things — and, by extension, for messages and news items
Measure Words.examples: 一条路 | yì tiáo lù | a road ; 一条河 | yì tiáo hé | a river ; 一条裤子 | yì tiáo kùzi | a pair of pants ; 一条鱼 | yì tiáo yú | a fish ; 一条消息 | yì tiáo xiāoxi | a message

Measure Words.notes: for tops/upper-body garments, and for abstract "matters" or "items of business"
Measure Words.examples: 一件衣服 | yí jiàn yīfu | a piece of clothing ; 一件事 | yí jiàn shì | a matter/thing that happened

Measure Words.notes: for most animals, and for one of a pair
Measure Words.examples: 一只猫 | yì zhī māo | a cat ; 一只鸟 | yì zhī niǎo | a bird ; 一只手 | yì zhī shǒu | one hand

Measure Words.notes: for things that come in natural pairs. Contrast 副 (fù) for sets like glasses
Measure Words.examples: 一双鞋 | yì shuāng xié | a pair of shoes ; 一双筷子 | yì shuāng kuàizi | a pair of chopsticks

Measure Words.notes: for sets/things worn in matched pieces
Measure Words.examples: 一副眼镜 | yí fù yǎnjìng | a pair of glasses ; 一副手套 | yí fù shǒutào | a pair of gloves

Measure Words.notes: for wheeled vehicles
Measure Words.examples: 一辆车 | yí liàng chē | a car ; 一辆自行车 | yí liàng zìxíngchē | a bicycle

Measure Words.notes: for machines and appliances — the "device" measure word
Measure Words.examples: 一台电视 | yì tái diànshì | a TV ; 一台电脑 | yì tái diànnǎo | a computer ; 一台冰箱 | yì tái bīngxiāng | a fridge

Measure Words.notes: for films, phones, and long works (novels, series)
Measure Words.examples: 一部电影 | yí bù diànyǐng | a movie ; 一部手机 | yí bù shǒujī | a cellphone ; 一部电视剧 | yí bù diànshìjù | a TV drama

Measure Words.notes: for events and performances that run for a stretch of time
Measure Words.examples: 一场电影 | yì chǎng diànyǐng | a movie showing ; 一场雨 | yì chǎng yǔ | a rainfall ; 一场演出 | yì chǎng yǎnchū | a performance

Measure Words.notes: for counting occurrences of an action — "times"
Measure Words.examples: 去过三次 | qù guo sān cì | been there three times ; 第一次 | dì yī cì | the first time

Measure Words.notes: for meals, and for scoldings/beatings
Measure Words.examples: 一顿饭 | yí dùn fàn | a meal ; 一顿火锅 | yí dùn huǒguō | a hotpot meal

Measure Words.notes: for cupfuls/glassfuls
Measure Words.examples: 一杯茶 | yì bēi chá | a cup of tea ; 一杯奶茶 | yì bēi nǎichá | a milk tea

Measure Words.notes: for bottlefuls
Measure Words.examples: 一瓶水 | yì píng shuǐ | a bottle of water

Measure Words.notes: for bowlfuls
Measure Words.examples: 一碗米饭 | yì wǎn mǐfàn | a bowl of rice

Measure Words.notes: for plates/dishes of food
Measure Words.examples: 一盘菜 | yì pán cài | a plate of food

Measure Words.notes: for portions, servings, and copies of documents
Measure Words.examples: 一份外卖 | yí fèn wàimài | a takeout order ; 一份工作 | yí fèn gōngzuò | a job ; 一份报纸 | yí fèn bàozhǐ | a newspaper

Measure Words.notes: for chunks/pieces — and the spoken word for units of money
Measure Words.examples: 一块蛋糕 | yí kuài dàngāo | a piece of cake ; 五块钱 | wǔ kuài qián | five yuan

Measure Words.notes: for things you grab by a handle
Measure Words.examples: 一把伞 | yì bǎ sǎn | an umbrella ; 一把椅子 | yì bǎ yǐzi | a chair ; 一把刀 | yì bǎ dāo | a knife

Measure Words.notes: for groups/crowds
Measure Words.examples: 一群人 | yì qún rén | a crowd of people ; 一群狗 | yì qún gǒu | a pack of dogs

Measure Words.notes: an indefinite "some/a few" — never takes a number other than 一
Measure Words.examples: 一些朋友 | yìxiē péngyou | some friends ; 这些 | zhèxiē | these ; 那些 | nàxiē | those

Measure Words.notes: a small indefinite amount — "a bit of". Note 有点儿 (a bit, before adjectives) vs 一点儿 (after them)
Measure Words.examples: 一点儿水 | yìdiǎnr shuǐ | a bit of water

Objects.notes: 半 goes before the measure word here. 半小时 (without 个) is also correct and common in writing.
Covers organized events and activities generally; as a verb it means to move around/stretch your legs.
个 is usual in casual speech but optional — 一小时 is perfectly standard, especially in writing (一小时后 = in an hour). 钟头 (zhōngtóu) is the casual northern alternative.
Also the verb "to wrap" — 包饺子 = to wrap dumplings.
起床 (qǐchuáng) = to get out of bed.
酒 (jiǔ) is the general word for alcohol.
Literally "self-propelled vehicle." 单车 (dānchē) in southern usage.
看书 = to read (literally "look at a book").
Also covers vehicles generally — 打车 = to hail a cab, 开车 = to drive.
手 (hand) + 机 (machine) — the everyday word; 电话 (diànhuà) is a phone call or a landline.
肉 (ròu) = meat; attach it to the animal — 牛肉 beef, 猪肉 pork, 羊肉 lamb.
The general word for clothes. 件 (jiàn) counts tops and single garments; 条 (tiáo) counts pants and skirts.
Loanword, both syllables first tone.
电 (electric) + 脑 (brain).
包饺子 = to make dumplings, a whole social activity in itself.
鸡 (chicken) + 蛋 (egg).
电 (electric) + 梯 (ladder/stairs). 坐电梯 = to take the elevator. 楼梯 (lóutī) = stairs, 扶梯 (fútī) = escalator.
Also the verb "to spend" (花钱 = to spend money) — same character.
could be online or in person
火 (fire) + 锅 (pot) — the popular communal dish.
Note the tone difference from 收拾 (shōushi, to tidy up) — same syllables, different tones.
Second syllable is neutral tone.
多少钱? = how much does it cost?
电 (electric) + 影 (shadow). 看电影 = to watch a movie.
面 alone can mean flour, noodles, or surface depending on context.
Takes 条 (tiáo) like other long, hanging things.
充电 (to charge) + 器 (device). 充电宝 (chōngdiànbǎo) = a power bank.
机 (machine/aircraft) + 票 (ticket). Easy to confuse with 季票 (jìpiào, season pass) further down this sheet — listen carefully for jì vs jī.
爆 (to pop/explode) + 米 (rice) + 花 (flower) — literally "exploded rice flower."
Cooked/steamed rice specifically (vs. 米 = uncooked rice grain).
烤 (roasted) + 鸭 (duck) — as in 北京烤鸭 (Peking duck).
don't confuse with 机票 jīpiào = plane ticket
配菜 pèicài = side dish
Careful with 糖 (táng, sugar) — same syllable, different tone.
地 (ground/earth) + 铁 (iron/rail).
火 (fire) + 车 (vehicle) — a holdover name from steam trains. Measure words: 列 (liè) for the train as a whole, 辆 for a single carriage, 趟 or 班 for a scheduled service.
Pronounced lèsè in Taiwan — a well-known cross-strait split.
电 (electric) + 视 (to view). The set and the medium both; 电视机 (diànshìjī) specifies the physical set.
节目 = a program/show. For a scripted drama series specifically, 电视剧 (diànshìjù) is what people actually say.
钱 (money) + 包 (bag).
Basic noun, root of 水果 (fruit) and 游泳 (to swim).

Places.notes: 国 (country) + 外 (outside). 出国 (chūguó) = to go abroad.
机 (aircraft) + 场 (field). Same 机 as 手机 and 机票.
Note the reading: 行 is háng here, not xíng.
酒 (alcohol) + 吧 (a phonetic "bar"). 清吧 = a quiet bar, 夜店 = a nightclub.
The room at home with the shower/tub. 洗澡 (xǐzǎo) = to bathe/shower is the verb that goes with it.
Literally "wash-hands room" — the polite term you ask for in a restaurant or shop. 厕所 (cèsuǒ) is blunter but completely normal; 卫生间 (wèishēngjiān) is the neutral written/signage word.
海 (sea) + 滩 (shore). 沙滩 (shātān) = sandy beach.
卧 (to lie down) + 室 (room). 两室一厅 (two bedrooms, one living room) is how apartments get advertised.
a more formal, structural sense — you'd use it talking about architecture as a subject, or a notable structure, not casually pointing at where you live
general, everyday word for "building" (also does double duty for "floor," as in 二楼 = 2nd floor)
公交车 (gōngjiāochē) = city bus. 站 (zhàn) is the shared "stop/station" element — 火车站, 地铁站, 公交站.
咖啡馆 (kāfēiguǎn) is a touch more established-sounding; both are used.
国 (country) + 家 — the same 家 as home.
农村 (nóngcūn) = rural village areas, slightly more neutral/formal.
literally "city center." This is the standard word for downtown. There is no Chinese equivalent of "uptown"
The sports ground/track at a school. 运动场 (yùndòngchǎng) is the general athletic field; 健身房 (jiànshēnfáng) is an indoor gym.
健身 (to work out) + 房 (room). 去健身房 = to go to the gym.
理发店 (lǐfàdiàn) — the general, everyday word for a hair salon/barbershop, for haircuts. 美发店 (měifàdiàn) — leans more toward styling (blowouts, dye, treatments), a bit trendier-sounding than 理发店.
走 (to walk) + 廊 (corridor). Inside an apartment, the short passage is usually 过道 (guòdào).

家 is fully locative in everyday use — 我在家, 回家, 你家很大. The contrast with 房子 is household/residence vs. the physical structure, not concept vs. place. It also means family, and doubles as the measure word for businesses.
酒店 leans upscale; 宾馆 (bīnguǎn) and 旅馆 (lǚguǎn) are more modest.
The physical structure/property, as opposed to 家 (jiā), which is the home as a household. 买房子 = to buy a place.
specifically implies a larger building (an office tower, a big complex)
图书 (books) + 馆 — the same 馆 as 博物馆, 餐馆.
客 (guest) + 厅 (hall) — the room where you receive people.
购物中心 (gòuwù zhōngxīn) = shopping center, a bit more formal.
菜市场 (càishìchǎng) = the wet/produce market specifically.
爬山 (páshān) = to go hiking.
电影 (movie) + 院 (courtyard/institution) — the same 院 as in 医院.
The gated residential complex most city apartments sit in — a unit of daily life with no clean English equivalent.
办公 (to do office work) + 室 (room).
公 (public) + 园 (garden).
药 (medicine) + 店 (shop).
The basic, general word for place - 什么地方 (what place/where), 这个地方 (this place).
The general word. 饭馆 (fànguǎn) is homier, 餐馆 (cānguǎn) sits in between.
a shop that sells that thing
逛街 (guàngjiē) = to go out shopping, literally "stroll the street." 路 (lù) is the other common word for road.
地 (ground/earth) + 铁 (iron/rail).
though people usually just say 酒吧 jiǔbā or 夜店 yèdiàn

Familiar People.notes: means boyfriend, specifically a romantic partner. For a platonic male friend, you'd say 男性朋友 (nánxìng péngyou)
a platonic male friend
Also commonly used as a friendly way to address a student/young person you don't know.
口 counts people in a household headcount (我家有五口人) — it attaches to 人, not to 家人 itself.
means girlfriend, specifically a romantic partner. For a platonic female friend, you'd say 女性朋友 (nǚxìng péngyou)
a platonic female friend

is gender-neutral and vaguer on purpose. Literally it means "object/target" (as in the object of one's affection), and it doesn't commit to specifics — it doesn't say whether you're married, dating, or how serious things are, and it doesn't specify the partner's gender. You'll hear it a lot from parents/relatives asking 你有对象了吗? (do you have a partner yet?) — it's the natural way to ask about someone's romantic status without presuming anything.
An adjective/state, not a person — 我是单身 or 我单身. 单身狗 (dānshēn gǒu, "single dog") is the self-deprecating slang.
Literally the person on my heart/mind - a warm, slightly literary/poetic way to refer to a romantic partner, softer than 男朋友/女朋友 or 对象.

Familiar People.english: to be in a romantic relationship
Familiar People.notes: 谈恋爱 tán liàn'ài = to date / be dating

Familiar People.english: to break up (romantic or close relationship)
Familiar People.notes: Literally means to part hands.
婚 on its own is a bound form — it lives inside 结婚, 离婚, 求婚 rather than standing alone. 婚姻 is the free-standing noun for marriage as an institution.
结 (to tie/form) + 婚 (marriage).
求 (to seek/ask for) + 婚 (marriage)

in China, traditionally means "spouse", but in Taiwan it can carry a connotation of a romantic partner outside a formal or married relationship (sometimes even implying an affair), rather than "my husband/wife."
Second syllable neutral. 交朋友 = to make friends.
The everyday, affectionate word. 丈夫 (zhàngfu) is the formal/written one you would use on a form.
Everyday and affectionate, mirroring 老公. 妻子 (qīzi) is the formal counterpart.
母亲 (mǔqīn) is the formal "mother."
父亲 (fùqīn) is the formal "father."
父 (father) + 母 (mother) — the compound is the normal word for parents.
Chinese splits siblings by age, always — there is no age-neutral "brother."
Also used warmly for a slightly older woman you are friendly with.
小孩 (xiǎohái) is the more casual "kid."
Chinese distinguishes the two sides: 奶奶 is your father's mother, 外婆 (wàipó) or 姥姥 (lǎolao) your mother's.
Mother's father is 外公 (wàigōng) or 姥爷 (lǎoye).
室 (room) + 友 (friend). Same 友 as 朋友, 网友 (online friend).
The go-to word for a woman's closest female friend — warmer and more specific than 好朋友.
The straightforward way to say it; 死党 (sǐdǎng) is the slangier "ride-or-die."
前 (former) + 任 (post/term) — literally "the previous occupant of the role." 前男友 / 前女友 spell out ex-boyfriend / ex-girlfriend.
暗 (secret/dark) + 恋 (to love) — specifically an unspoken one-sided crush.
The moment you tell someone you like them. A distinct, named event in Chinese dating vocabulary.
我们在一起了 = we're together now, the standard way to announce a relationship.
介绍…给… = to introduce someone to someone.

Professional.notes: Also used to address shop owners/proprietors directly, even ones you don't work for.
Also the standard respectful form of address — you call a teacher 王老师 rather than by name alone.
收银 (to take payment) + 员 (staff member). The 员 suffix builds a lot of job titles: 服务员, 演员, 售货员.
服务 (service) + 员. Also what you call out to get service in a restaurant.
保 (to protect) + 安 (safety) — the security guard at an apartment complex or office, which is who a "doorman" usually is. 门卫 (ménwèi) is the gatekeeper at an entrance specifically.
同 (same) + 事 (work/matter). Same 同 as 同学 (classmate).
会 alone is a bound form living inside 开会 (to have a meeting) and 会员; 会议 is the free-standing noun. 会 also separately means "can/know how to."
This is the person, not the status — 会员卡 (huìyuánkǎ) = membership card, 办会员 = to sign up for a membership.
请 (to request) + 假 (leave). You ask your boss for this. Contrast 放假 (the institution gives it) and 休假 (you are taking it).
放 (to release) + 假. Used for holidays and school breaks — 放假了! is what you say when term ends.

Professional.english: to go on a business trip
Professional.notes: 出 (to go out) + 差 (assignment).
A manual/factory worker specifically. 员工 (yuángōng) = employee/staff of a company, which is the word you want for office work.
The neutral, respectful term — 性 (sex) + 工作者 (worker). The 工作者 suffix marks the profession as a profession.
Gender-neutral, covers actor and actress. 男演员 / 女演员 specify when needed; 明星 (míngxīng) = a star/celebrity.

Professional.english: to give a speech / talk at people
Professional.notes: The everyday "to speak/address people." 演讲 (yǎnjiǎng) is a prepared formal speech or lecture.
开 (to open/start) + 会. 我在开会 = I'm in a meeting.
To be on leave/vacation — the state, as opposed to 请假 (asking for it) and 放假 (being granted it). 我在休假 = I'm off right now.
Both the noun and the verb — 我在工作 (I'm working), 找工作 (to look for a job).
The 师 suffix marks skilled professions: 老师, 律师, 工程师.
数据 (data) + 工程师. 数据分析 (shùjù fēnxī) = data analysis, 数据库 (shùjùkù) = database.
客人 (kèrén) is a guest or a customer in a shop; 客户 is the business-relationship sense.
上 (to go up/onto) + 班 (shift). Mirror of 下班.
下班了 = done for the day.
加 (to add) + 班 (shift).
辞 (to dismiss/take leave of) + 职 (post).
This is what the company does — 公司裁员了. To say you were laid off, use the passive: 我被裁了 / 被裁员了.
面 (face) + 试 (test). Also a verb: 我明天面试.
简 (brief) + 历 (history/record).
升 (to rise) + 职 (post).
截止 (to cut off) + 日期 (date). In tech offices, the English "deadline" or DDL is used constantly too.
The word for reporting up to a manager — 向老板汇报.
Not a physical office — the world of work as a whole: 职场文化 (workplace culture), 职场新人 (someone new to working life).

Body.notes: 对……过敏 (duì...guòmǐn, "to be allergic to ___")
金色 ("gold-colored") is the natural way to describe blonde hair in Mandarin — there's no separate word borrowed for "blonde." 头发 = hair.
多 + verb here means "more of" the action — 多休息 = rest more/get plenty of rest.
不太舒服 is the standard mild way to say you're feeling off, without specifying what's wrong.
好多了 = a big improvement from before — the 了 marks the change from how things were.
注意 = pay attention to; 身体 = body/health. A warm, common send-off, especially to someone older or unwell.
中 (Chinese) + 医 (medicine). 西医 (xīyī) = Western medicine, the term it exists in contrast to.

Body.english: to be discharged from the hospital
Body.notes: 出 (to exit) + 院 (hospital). 住院 (zhùyuàn) = to be admitted/hospitalized.
literally means "look at the sickness"
背 (bèi) = the upper back. Chinese splits the back in two: 腰 (yāo) is the lower back/waist, and 腰疼 is a different complaint entirely.
Both noun and verb. 多休息 = get plenty of rest, as in 你多休息 above.
生病 = to fall ill. The 了 marks the change of state — you weren't sick, now you are.
The colloquial belly — what hurts, what gets full (肚子饱了). 胃 (wèi) is the stomach organ specifically, as in 胃疼 or 胃不好.
The upper back. Note the reading: 背 is bèi as a noun but bēi as the verb "to carry on one's back."
大腿 = thigh, 小腿 = calf — Chinese builds them off the same root.
Goes after the body part, not before: 头疼, 背疼, 肚子疼. 痛 (tòng) means the same thing and dominates in writing and in Taiwan.
头 (head) + 发 (hair) — only hair on the head. 毛 (máo) covers body and animal hair. Second syllable is neutral tone here, though 发 is fā elsewhere.
Neutral tone on the second syllable — this is the pair that trips everyone up against 眼镜 (glasses).
眼镜 (jìng, 4th tone) = glasses vs 眼睛 (jing, neutral) = eyes. Near-identical to the ear at speed; the tone is the whole difference. 戴眼镜 = to wear glasses.
Built the same way as 心情好 — just negate the adjective. 心情很差 (chà) is stronger.
累死了 (lèi sǐ le, "tired to death") is the everyday exaggeration.
睡 (to sleep) + 觉 (sleep, as a thing) — a verb-object pair, so things split them: 睡了一个好觉.
Sleepy/drowsy — the state before sleeping, distinct from 累 (physically tired).
洗脸 = to wash your face. Also carries the social sense — 丢脸 (diūliǎn) = to lose face.
The body part; 口 (kǒu) is the more abstract "mouth/opening" that shows up in compounds and as a measure word.
刷牙 = to brush teeth. 牙医 (yáyī) = dentist.
Distinct from 腿 (leg) — Chinese does not blur them.
手 (hand) + 指 (to point).
发 (to emit) + 烧 (to burn).
Both the illness and the verb — 我感冒了 = I've come down with a cold.
Also used figuratively for anything that gives you grief — 这件事很头疼.
嗓子 = throat/voice.
吃药 = to take medicine (Chinese "eats" medicine, whatever the form).
受 (to receive) + 伤 (injury).
Both "to exercise" and "sports" as a noun.
减 (to reduce) + 肥 (fat).
个子高 = tall, 个子矮 = short. 身高 (shēngāo) is the measured number.
Noun and verb both — 我感觉不太好.
Single syllable, fourth tone — 我饿了.

Activities.notes: 合 (to combine) + 菜 (dishes) — shared dishes eaten together, as opposed to individual plates. Your note describes this as 大家一起吃 ("everyone eats together"), which is more a descriptive phrase than a fixed term.
could be online or in person
Trekking/hiking as a named activity, a bit sporty and modern in feel.
爬 (to climb) + 山 (mountain). The default word for going hiking in China, even on gentle hills — where English says "hike," Mandarin usually says "climb a mountain."

Activities.english: to give a speech / talk at people

Activities.notes: 外卖 = takeout
游 (to swim/roam) + 泳 (swimming).
单身 (single) + 派对 (party, a loanword). 派对 is the transliteration; 聚会 (jùhuì) is the native word for a get-together.
The fifth day of the fifth lunar month — dragon boat races and 粽子 (zòngzi, sticky rice parcels).
To watch closely/observe something or someone. For observing a holiday or custom, the verb is just 过 — 过节 (to celebrate a festival).
筹 (to raise/gather) + 款 (funds). 募捐 (mùjuān) is soliciting donations specifically; 众筹 (zhòngchóu) = crowdfunding.
The direct term. 性 (xìng) alone is sex as a concept/topic; 上床 (shàngchuáng, "go to bed") is the common euphemism, roughly like "sleep with."
To take part in something organized — 参加婚礼, 参加活动, 参加比赛.
A transliteration of "talk show" that in practice means stand-up comedy in China. 相声 (xiàngsheng) is traditional two-person crosstalk; 喜剧 (xǐjù) is comedy as a genre.
租房 = to rent a place, 房租 (fángzū) = the rent you pay, 出租 = to rent out (hence 出租车, taxi).
脱 is the mirror of 穿 (chuān, to put on). Also 脱鞋 = to take shoes off, which you do indoors.
跳 (to jump) + 舞 (dance). A genuine verb-object pair, so things slot between the halves: 跳个舞 (have a dance), 跳了一支舞 (danced one dance).
To live/reside somewhere — 我住在纽约. For "to live" in the sense of one's life, that's 生活 (shēnghuó), which is also the noun "life."
听音乐 = to listen to music. 听说 = to hear that…, 听懂 = to understand by listening.
The general "to do/make." 干 (gàn) is the colloquial equivalent (你在干什么?), and 办 (bàn) is to handle/get something done (办事).
晚饭 = dinner. 做饭 on its own = to cook (a meal), which is what you say most of the time.
午饭 = lunch; 早饭 (zǎofàn) = breakfast.
The general one — covers cooking any meal.
Also just "to eat" generally. 吃了吗? ("eaten yet?") works as a casual greeting.
喝酒 = to drink alcohol, 喝茶 = to drink tea.
唱 (to sing) + 歌 (song). KTV is the social default for this.
跑 (to run) + 步 (step).
旅行 (lǚxíng) is closer to "to travel" as a journey; 旅游 leans toward tourism/vacationing.
逛 (to stroll) + 街 (street) — browsing as an outing. 购物 (gòuwù) is the transactional "to shop."
Literally "look at a book" — this is how you say "to read" as a pastime. 读 (dú) is to read aloud or study a text.
开 (to operate/open) + 车. Same 开 as 开会, 开门.
骑 is the verb for anything you straddle — bikes, motorcycles, horses.
健 (healthy) + 身 (body). 健身房 = gym.
拍 (to snap) + 照 (photo). 照片 (zhàopiàn) = the photo itself.
打 is the verb for games and ball sports — 打篮球, 打游戏. 玩 (wán) is to play more generally.
弹 for plucked/keyed instruments — 弹钢琴, 弹吉他. 吹 (chuī) for wind instruments, 拉 (lā) for bowed ones.
等一下 = hold on a second.
打 again — 给我打电话 = call me.
发 (to send out) + 消息 (message). 发微信 = to message on WeChat.
买 (mǎi, 3rd tone) vs 卖 (mài, 4th tone) — the tone is the only difference between buying and selling.
See 买 above; keep the tones straight.
付 (to pay) + 钱 (money). 买单 (mǎidān) = to settle the bill at a restaurant.

Activities.english: to drink tea / hang out at a teahouse
Activities.notes: In Cantonese-speaking regions 饮茶/喝茶 also means going out for dim sum.
Both the noun (a gathering) and the verb. The native counterpart to 派对.
The everyday way to propose doing something together — 周末出去玩吧.

Directions.notes: The suffix that turns a bare direction into a standalone place word: 上面, 下面, 里面, 外面, 前面, 后面. 边 (biān) is the interchangeable alternative.
Chinese has no everyday equivalent of a city "block" — directions count intersections instead: 往前走两个路口 = go two blocks. 街区 (jiēqū) exists but is not what people say.
对 (facing) + 面 — across from/opposite: 在马路对面. The verb "to cross" is 过 (guò) or 穿过 (chuānguò).
Bound the same way — 后面 / 后边 = behind. 以后 = after (in time).
A bound locative — it needs 面 or 边 to stand alone: 下面 / 下边 = below. 下 by itself is the verb "to go down" (下楼, 下班, 下雨).
在拐角 = at the corner. 角落 (jiǎoluò) is an interior corner of a room.
方 does not mean "side" on its own — it lives inside 地方 (place), 方向 (direction), 南方 (the south). The word for side is 边 (biān).
The preposition for measuring gaps: 我家离公司很近.
A location — 我在楼下 = I'm downstairs. Also used for "outside my building," which is how people say they've arrived.
东边 / 东面 to stand alone.
离……很远 = far from…
从……到…… = from…to…. 从这里到那里.
Bound — 前面 / 前边 = in front. 以前 = before (in time).
The action of going down. Note the flip: 楼下 (place) vs 下楼 (motion) — same two characters, reversed.
The action of going up, mirroring 下楼.
这儿 (zhèr) is the northern equivalent. 那里 / 那儿 = there.
Asks for the route on foot/by any means: 去地铁站怎么走? = how do I get to the subway station?
Asks by what means — subway, taxi, walking. 怎么走 wants the route; 怎么去 wants the method.
在……中间 = between/among. Takes two reference points: 在银行和超市中间.
里边 is the same word. 在里面 = inside.
Bound like the others — 左边 (zuǒbian) = the left side, 往左 = to the left.
地 (ground) + 图 (diagram).
英 marks it as the English/imperial unit. In practice China measures in 公里 (gōnglǐ, kilometers); 里 (lǐ) alone is the traditional Chinese unit, about half a kilometer.
离……很近 = close to…
在……旁边 = next to. 在我旁边 = next to me.
北京 = northern capital, 南京 = southern capital.
在桌子上面 = on top of the table. In practice 上 alone often suffices: 桌子上.
外边 is the same word. 在外面吃 = to eat out.
右边 (yòubian) = the right side. Chinese always names them in the order 左右, which is also the word for "approximately."
This, not 方, is the actual word for "side." Interchangeable with 面 as a locative suffix: 左边/左面, 里边/里面.
Chinese recites the compass as 东南西北, and the combinations reverse English: 东北 = northeast, 西南 = southwest.
那儿 (nàr) in the north. 哪里 (nǎlǐ, where) differs only in tone — listen for nǎ vs nà.
Also a verb, "to arrive" — 我到了 = I'm here. 到了 = arrived.
迷 (to be confused) + 路 (road).
直 (straight) + 走. 一直走 = keep going straight.
Literally "to sit" — 坐地铁, 坐火车, 坐飞机. 骑 for bikes, 开 for driving yourself.
打 again. 打的 (dǎdī) is the older slang; ride apps mostly killed street hailing anyway.
换 (to change) + 乘 (to ride). On signage everywhere in subways.
拐 (guǎi) = to turn a corner. 左转 (zuǒ zhuǎn) is the more formal/driving-instruction version.
Mirror of the above.
走路去 = to go on foot.
往前走 = keep going forward, 往左拐 = turn left. 向 (xiàng) is the slightly more formal alternative.
A location — 在楼上.
东西 (dōngxi, east-west) as a compound means "thing/stuff" — a useful accident to remember.
哪里 / 哪儿 — 儿 forms are northern/Beijing-flavored, 里 forms more universal. Careful with 那里 (nàlǐ, there): 哪 (nǎ) asks, 那 (nà) points.

Descriptions.notes: Also very common with time: 大约三点 (dàyuē sān diǎn, around 3 o'clock), 大约一个小时 (about an hour).
左右 goes after the number (十个左右 = 10-ish), and feels a bit more casual/spoken.
Very versatile — can praise someone's skill ("you're amazing") or describe something intense/severe depending on context and tone.
Basic temperature adjective, opposite of 热 (hot).
Basic temperature adjective, opposite of 冷 (cold).
Used to soften a comparison, e.g. 比较好 (relatively good/pretty good).
Basic flavor adjective.
The opposite of 脏 (zāng). 打扫干净 = to clean something until it is clean — 干净 works as a result complement.
金色 ("gold-colored") is the natural way to describe blonde hair in Mandarin — there's no separate word borrowed for "blonde." 头发 = hair.
Placed before a color for a bright, eye-catching, almost neon effect — 亮黄色 (neon yellow), 亮粉色 (neon pink). 亮 on its own also just means "bright/shiny" (e.g. for lights).
Placed before a color to mean "dark/deep" — 深蓝色, 深红色. Also means "deep" generally (深水) and "profound."
深 + 蓝色 — a very common way to say "navy/dark blue," for clothes, cars, ink, etc.
Refers to the color gold, but is also the go-to word for describing blonde hair. Not used for the metal gold itself (that's 黄金, huángjīn).
Placed before a color to mean "light/pale" — 浅蓝色 (light blue), 浅绿色 (light green). The more universal of the two "light" modifiers.
Also means "light/pale," but leans toward a delicate, washed-out, or subtle shade — 淡黄色 (pale yellow), 淡紫色 (pale lavender). Often preferred for soft, muted tones; 浅 is more neutral/general-purpose.
色 is kept here because 橙 on its own means the orange fruit — the bare syllable would be ambiguous in a way 红/蓝/绿 are not.
淡 + 黄色 — a soft, muted yellow. 淡 fits here better than 浅 for this gentle, washed-out shade.
粉色 is the common everyday term; 粉红色 (fěnhóngsè, literally "powder-red") means the same thing and is a bit more descriptive/formal, but both are used interchangeably in speech.
The all-purpose word for red — also carries cultural weight (luck, celebration) in Chinese contexts.
Refers to the color silver (metallic or otherwise); for silver/gray hair specifically, 银发 (yínfà) is the more literary/set term.
Fantasy — magic, other worlds. 科幻 (kēhuàn) = sci-fi, 玄幻 (xuánhuàn) = Chinese-style fantasy with cultivation and immortals, 武侠 (wǔxiá) = martial-arts fiction.
最 is the superlative marker and goes before any adjective — 最大 (biggest), 最贵 (most expensive), 最喜欢 (favorite). 最好 also means "had better": 你最好早点去.
Also a friendly prefix for people younger than you — 小王.
Only for objects. For people, 老 (lǎo).
Also a familiar prefix — 老王, 老板, 老公.
Also "honored" in polite phrases — 您贵姓? = what is your (esteemed) surname?
Note the reading: 便 is pián here, not biàn as in 方便.
The all-purpose positive. Stacks onto verbs to form adjectives: 好吃, 好喝, 好看, 好玩.
好 + 吃 (to eat). For drinks it is 好喝 (hǎohē) — Chinese keeps them separate.
Works for people, clothes, movies — anything worth looking at.
For places and activities.
高兴 (gāoxìng) is close; 开心 is the more everyday "in good spirits."
难 (difficult) + 过 (to pass) — literally "hard to get through."
美 (měi) is more formal/aesthetic.
可 (-able) + 爱 (to love) — "loveable."
Also used for anything cool or slickly done.
Same character as in 难过 and 难看 (ugly).
Also "soon" — 快到了 = almost there. Do not confuse it with its homophone 块 (kuài), the spoken unit of money.
慢慢来 = take your time, one of the most-used phrases in the language.
Note the reading: cháng = long, zhǎng = to grow (长大).
For height, 矮 (ǎi).
For people and for heights/prices alike.
Also the verb "to quarrel" — 吵架 (chǎojià).
The same word as in 不太舒服 (feeling unwell) — comfort of body covers both.
方 (direction/way) + 便 (biàn here, not pián).
Also for personality/talk — 嘴甜 = sweet-talking.
Also describes sore muscles — 腰酸.
Also "hardship" — 辛苦了 uses it.
Literally "has meaning." 没意思 = boring, the everyday counterpart to 无聊.
重 (heavy) + 要 (to want/need).
免 (to exempt) + 费 (fee). Different from 有空 (free as in available).
Also the verb "to squeeze" — 挤地铁 = to cram onto the subway.
A loan from English "cool." Same character as in 酷儿 (queer).
an adjective meaning "all" that modifies a noun, while 都 (dōu) is an adverb meaning "both/all" that points back to a plural subject
an adverb meaning "both/all" that points back to a plural subject

Food.notes: used for food, air, experience, etc.

Food.english: to earn / to make a profit

Transition Words.notes: Always, habitually. 一直 (yìzhí) is "continuously/all along" — 一直在等 = have been waiting the whole time.

Your "formal/informal" split is softer than it looks: 经常 and 常常 are near-interchangeable, with 经常 the more common in speech and 常常 leaning slightly literary. The genuinely informal one is 老是 (lǎoshì — fourth tone; lǎoshi would be 老实, "honest"), which carries a complaining tone: 他老是迟到.
See 经常 above. 老是 (lǎoshì) is the casual, mildly exasperated version.
Sometimes. For "when I have time," 有空的时候 (yǒu kòng de shíhou) — 空 is free time, 时候 is the moment.
Less frequent than 有时候 — occasionally, now and then.
Literally "very few" — 我很少喝酒 = I rarely drink. 几乎不 (almost never) is the stronger form.
每 (every) + 隔 (to separate by): 每隔一天 = every other day, 每隔一周 = every other week.
For laying out points in order: 首先…其次…最后. In casual speech people just use 先 (xiān): 先吃饭, 然后…
The workhorse sequencer. 然后呢? = "and then?" keeps a story going.
最 (most) + 后 (after). Also just means "last/final" — 最后一天.
The mirror of 以后 (yǐhòu). It follows the event: 吃饭(event)以前 = before eating. On its own it means "in the past."
one of the most common function words in Mandarin, meaning "then" in conditionals, or "right away/already" depending on context.
Carries relief after a wait — different from 最后, which is just sequential.
It follows the event: 吃饭(event)以后 = after eating.
Wraps around a clause rather than introducing it: 我小的时候 = when I was little. The question word "when?" is 什么时候.
下次见 = see you next time.
一 shifts to yí before a fourth tone. Shortened to 上次 (shàng cì) in speech — the 一 usually drops. Same pattern for 这次, 下次.
几 covers small counts. 好几次 (hǎo jǐ cì) = quite a few times.
Nearly always pairs with a sentence-final 了: 我已经吃了.
后天 (hòutiān) = the day after tomorrow.
前天 (qiántiān) = the day before yesterday. Note how 前/后 map onto time the same way they map onto space.
以前 = before/previously (also row above); 过去 = the past as a stretch of time, and literally "to go over."
Describes how something was before a change - 我原本想去 (I originally wanted to go). Often sets up a contrast with what actually happened.
刚 (gāng) alone before a verb also means "just did": 我刚到.
Two common uses: still (我还是不明白 = I still dont understand); or in either-or questions (你要茶还是咖啡 = tea or coffee?). Traditional form is 還是.
跟我一起去 = come with me. 和 (hé) also works; 跟 is more spoken, especially in the north.
Joins nouns only — never two sentences. For linking clauses use 然后 (then) or 而且 (moreover).
The default reaction of mild surprise or interest — said constantly in conversation, much lighter than English "really?" can sound.
几次 expects a small number, 多少次 is open-ended. Note it overlaps with "a few times" — 几 both asks and answers.
多 (how) + 久 (long in time). 多长时间 (duō cháng shíjiān) means the same thing, a touch more explicit.
The everyday way to introduce an opinion or feeling — softer and more common in speech than 我认为.

Transition Words.english: it's like this / so here's the thing

Transition Words.notes: A hedge — "not necessarily / we'll see." Common as a standalone reply.
Softens a statement into an impression rather than a fact — sits before the thing it hedges: 好像下雨了 (seems like it's raining).
Verb "to give," and also the preposition "to/for" before the recipient: 给我打电话 = call me.
Goes after an adjective or verb: 贵一点儿 = a bit more expensive. Contrast 有点儿, which goes before and leans negative: 有点儿贵 = a bit too expensive.

Transition Words.hanzi: 我会 / 我要 / 我打算
Transition Words.pinyin: wǒ huì / wǒ yào / wǒ dǎsuàn
Transition Words.notes: Three different futures: 会 = will (prediction or ability), 要 = going to (intention, firm), 打算 = plan to (deliberate). Mandarin has no tense, so the choice of these carries it.
想 = would like, soft and safe for requests. 要 = want, firmer and can sound demanding — fine when ordering food, blunt when asking a favor.
待会儿 (dāihuìr) is the northern spoken equivalent.
Pairs with 但是 in the second clause — Chinese keeps both halves: 虽然…但是… where English drops one.
Often paired with 不但 (not only): 不但…而且…
For statements. 还是 (háishì) is for questions — 茶还是咖啡? Getting these backwards is the classic mistake.
Softens a correction — 其实我不太喜欢.
Dismisses the preceding complication: 反正我都可以.
Also the noun "result." Often introduces an unexpected outcome.
Restates or clarifies what you just said.
Said when something pops into your head mid-conversation. Literally "correct" — the pivot is idiomatic.
特别 alone = especially/particularly.
Pairs with 一方面 for a two-sided argument.
要是 is the spoken counterpart to 如果; 就 picks up the consequence.
For emphasis: 连我都知道 = even I know that.
一到就走 = left as soon as he arrived. Two very common function words doing a lot of work.
同 (same) + 时 (time).
More formal than 因为; common in writing.
Goes at the front: 为了省钱, 我自己做饭.
Very close to 原本 above — 本来 is the more common in speech.
Also "possible/possibility." 大概 (dàgài) and 应该 (yīnggāi) cover similar hedging ground.
Said on realizing why something was the case.

Transition Words.english: only then; not until; only (used for small amounts)

Daily Life.notes: 都可以 answers "which one/where/when" questions by saying every option is fine — interchangeable with 随便你 but slightly more neutral, less deferential.
有空 = to have free time. The standard opener for proposing to meet up.
生日快乐 = happy birthday.
早餐 (zǎocān) is the slightly more formal/menu word.
国产剧 (guóchǎnjù, "domestically produced drama") is what people actually say. Genres: 古装剧 (period/costume), 都市剧 (urban/contemporary). By the same pattern 韩剧 = K-drama, 美剧 = US shows, 日剧 = J-drama.
Basic word for a class/lesson.
Also means "embarrassed": 我不好意思说 = I'm too embarrassed to say.
过节 (guòjié) = to celebrate a holiday. 春节 = Spring Festival/Lunar New Year.
The universal shopping question.
The potential complement — 不 slots between verb and result to mean "cannot." 看不见 = unable to see vs 没看见 = didn't see. The positive form is 看得见 (can see).
见 as a result complement = perceived. 听见 (heard it) vs 听懂 (understood it) — you can do the first without the second, which is exactly the learner's situation.
Same pattern as 听见. 没 negates completed actions, never 不.

懂 is a result complement: 听懂 = understood by listening, 看懂 = understood by reading. 我不明白 (wǒ bù míngbai) is different — it means the idea itself does not make sense to you, not that you missed the words.
不知道 on its own is fine as a full reply.
听 (hear) + 说 (say) — "I heard it said that…". Introduces secondhand information: 我听说他要搬家.

Daily Life.english: I'll get it / let me handle it
Daily Life.notes: 我来 = I'll do it (the action is implied by context — paying the bill, carrying something, answering the door).
The standard reply to an apology or minor mishap — literally "no connection/relevance" (i.e., it doesn't matter).

Daily Life.english: it's like this / so here's the thing

Daily Life.notes: 说好了 = we've agreed on this already. Used to confirm a plan is locked in, sometimes with a light "no backing out" undertone.
Doubling the verb (想想) softens it into "have a little think" — a very common move in Mandarin.
改天 = some other day. A polite way to postpone plans without giving a firm reason.
中学 (middle/secondary school) + 生 (student). 小学生 = primary schooler, 大学生 = university student.
上午 (shàngwǔ) covers late morning up to noon.
Interchangeable with 没关系 in most situations; a touch more casual.

The natural everyday way to say other people/someone else - used constantly in casual speech. Contrast with 其他人 (qítārén), which leans toward the rest of the people in a specific group rather than people in general.
号码 = number (as an identifier). 手机号 (shǒujīhào) is the everyday short form.
改 (to change) + 天 (day) — "some other day." The polite soft-postpone, as in 我们改天吧.
For real apologies. 不好意思 (bù hǎoyìsi) is the lighter "excuse me / my bad," used far more often.
暴 (violent/sudden) + 雨 (rain). 台风 (táifēng) = typhoon, 雷阵雨 (léizhènyǔ) = thunderstorm.
谢谢你 adds the person. 不客气 (bú kèqi) = you're welcome.
夸张 = exaggerated. Used for reacting to something excessive, whether outrageous news or someone being dramatic.
For replying to a message, 回复 (huífù) or just 回.
问问题 = to ask a question. 请问 = "may I ask," the standard opener to a stranger.
Three "cans": 可以 (permitted), 会 (learned skill), 能 (physically able).
空 is kòng (free time) here, not kōng (empty). 没空 = busy/not available.
迟 (late) + 到 (to arrive).
生 (to produce) + 气 (air/temper). Two patterns: 对我生气 or the split form 生我的气 — the possessive slots inside the verb.
带伞 = bring an umbrella. Also "to lead" — 带你去.
换钱 = to exchange money, 换衣服 = to change clothes.
Split from your combined "打扫 / 收拾" entry. Usually implies sweeping/cleaning a space (floors, surfaces).
Same 洗 as 洗脸, 洗澡, 洗手.
我忘了 = I forgot.
送 covers giving as a gift and seeing someone off — 送你回家 = to walk you home. For simply handing something over, 给 (gěi).
去 (to go there) vs 来 (lái, to come here) — Chinese picks the verb by where the speaker is standing. 去年 = last year.
回 (to return). 回来 = to come back, 回去 = to go back.
帮我一下 = give me a hand. 帮忙 (bāngmáng) is the verb-object form: 帮我一个忙.
赶时间 = to be pressed for time, 赶紧 (gǎnjǐn) = quickly, right away.
Contrast 认识 (to know a person). 我不知道 = I don't know.
Also the noun: 有什么安排? = what are your plans?
外卖 = takeout
认识 = to know/be acquainted with a person or place. 知道 (zhīdào) = to know a fact. 我认识他 vs 我知道他 are different claims.
看 does a lot of work: 看书 (read), 看电影 (watch), 看病 (see a doctor), 看看 (take a look).
分 also means "minute" and "point/score," and 分手 (to break up) is literally "to part hands."
开 spans open/start/operate: 开门, 开会, 开车, 开始.
Three senses: to think, to miss someone (我想你), and to want to (想去).
扔垃圾 = to take out the trash.
leans toward organizing/putting things away rather than scrubbing. Note the tone difference from 首饰 (shǒushi, jewelry) above — easy to mix up.
试试看 = give it a try. 试衣服 = to try on clothes.
明白了 = got it. 懂了 (dǒng le) works the same way.
不用 (búyòng) = no need — a very common polite refusal.
随便 on its own means "whatever/however"; adding 你 makes it explicitly about deferring to the other person's choice.
微 (micro) + 信 (message). 加微信 = to add someone on WeChat, the standard way to exchange contacts.
那 here refers back to whatever was just mentioned; 还好 softens a judgment to "could be worse."
几 asks for a small number, so it is the right question word for the hour. Answer with 点: 三点半 = 3:30, 三点一刻 = 3:15.
说得对 uses 得 to attach the result (对, correct) to the verb 说 — literally "what you said comes out correct."

Daily Life.english: You've worked hard / thanks for the effort
Daily Life.notes: Said to acknowledge someone's effort or hardship — after a long shift, a big task, or a hard trip. No single-word English equivalent.
